gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1015r:
Treasury Continues to Maintain Its Formal Process to Promote U.S. Policies at the International Monetary Fund, GAO-05-1015R of September 14, 2005, is a yearly check set by Congress. Law gives the United States dozens of set aims at the Fund. In 2003 and 2004, GAO counted nearly 70 such mandates. They cover trade, human rights, terror finance, and arms spread.

GAO tracks the formal steps Treasury set up in 1999 to push those aims. It checks how U.S. votes and voice are used at the Fund's board. The process still stands, the title notes. Proof of direct U.S. sway stays hard to pin down, since the Fund acts by broad accord.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1055r:
Agency Telework Methodologies, GAO-05-1055R of September 27, 2005, sends Congress a briefing on how five agencies run work-from-home plans. The five are the Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the Small Business Administration, and the Securities and Exchange Commission. Staff briefed Congress on July 29, 2005. The letter puts that briefing on paper.

For each agency, GAO shows three things. It shows how the agency picks who may work from home. It shows how staff learn of and claim that chance. It shows how each agency counts who takes part. Side-by-side facts let readers spot strong and weak ways to run such plans.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-265r:
Catalogue of Federal Insurance Activities, GAO-05-265R of March 4, 2005, lists a risk the budget hides in plain sight. The federal government bears loss risk for a wide spread of work. For flood aid, it bears the whole risk. For jobless aid and some work claims, it shares the risk with states or firms. No one list has named it all.

No shared sense of what counts as federal insurance exists. Risk hides in funds whose names tell of other work. GAO hunts it down line by line here. The list sorts risk by the kinds firms know: health, life, disability, and property loss.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-505r:
Future Farmers of America, also known as the National FFA Organization, is covered by GAO letter GAO-05-505R, dated June 10, 2005. The group funds scholarships and awards for young people in farming. It runs a national convention and provides education services. The audit reports at issue cover the fiscal years ended August 31, 2003, and August 31, 2002.

Federal charter law obliges the group to issue yearly financial statements and to obtain an outside audit. GAO's role was to read the audit reports and alert Congress to any failure to follow the law's reporting terms. Staff read the statements and their notes and ran analytical procedures on the figures. No instance of noncompliance was identified. In the auditors' opinion the statements were presented fairly under generally accepted accounting principles. GAO did not review the auditors' working papers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-545r:
Defense work on high energy lasers is checked against Congress's orders in a GAO letter, GAO-05-545R, dated May 18, 2005. A 2000 law told the department to draft a master plan for laser weapons work. The plan called for a new management setup and a better balance of spending. Big demonstration projects were to share funds more evenly with basic science and technology work. A 2001 law ordered the setup put in place.

GAO found the department has largely followed that direction. A joint office now sets priorities through a clear process that draws on expert views. Teamwork across the laser field has grown under the new structure. Spending balance has shifted as well. In 1998 the science base took 17 percent of laser spending, $66 million of $398 million. By 2004 it took 27 percent, $263 million of $983 million. Services still fund projects by their own missions. The letter reports a program steered back toward the plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-595r:
Agriculture's turn in this audit series comes in GAO-05-595R, a letter GAO issued on July 22, 2005. It covers the department's management representation letter for fiscal year 2004. That letter supports the audit of the government's consolidated financial statements. GAO found needed improvements in two of the five key areas it reviewed, and none in the matter of thresholds.

The letter held 28 of the 29 standard representations that applied to the department. The one remaining representation was not provided at all. Finance officials later said they had believed a disclosure covered it. The second fault concerned uncorrected errors. The summary sent with the letter was incomplete, and it carried no description of the misstatements. GAO made two recommendations to the acting chief financial officer. The inspector general was asked to work with the department on future letters. Both offices said they will address the points raised.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-715r:
Military moving costs pass a recheck in GAO letter GAO-05-715R, sent June 9, 2005. The defense department spends over $1.7 billion a year moving troops' household goods, over 600,000 shipments. Reforms drawn from pilot programs were priced at 13 percent above current costs, and Congress doubted the figure. The program's record includes long-standing complaints about lost and damaged property. The department redid the math and stress-tested it. In its simulations, the reforms cost 15 percent or less above current spending about 80 percent of the time.

GAO calls the method sound and the answers responsive. The department agreed with the letter's account.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-765r:
Munitions planning is revisited in letter GAO-05-765R, dated August 12, 2005. In 2002, GAO found a weak link between what field commanders need soon and what the services buy. The Defense Department agreed to fix the gap. It rewrote its core instruction in October 2003. GAO now checked whether the new rules work in practice.

GAO found the link exists on paper but not in practice. Few offices followed the new timeline and coordination duties. In the Korea command's war plan stock, key dates were missed. Threat reports that shape target lists came late. Staff had to work from dated facts. GAO held that commanders' needs still require a real link to buying choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1135r:
Land values in a proposed Oregon land swap are questioned in GAO-06-1135R, a letter report dated September 26, 2006. Bill H.R. 5025 would trade private land and business interests at Cooper Spur for Forest Service land at Government Camp. Two appraisal reports support the swap's terms. Congress asked GAO whether those reports met known appraisal standards. The tests were industry standards and the federal rules for land purchases. GAO briefed congressional staff on September 21, 2006.

Two review appraisers checked the reports' data, logic, and consistency. They did not inspect the sites or set their own values. Both agreed that the Cooper Spur report failed to meet the standards. They split on whether the Government Camp report complied. GAO concluded that the government has limited assurance that either report reflects true market value. The letter matters because a bad appraisal can shortchange the public in a land trade.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-155r:
Competition in the small group health insurance market is measured state by state in GAO-06-155R, a letter report dated October 13, 2005. Congress asked for an update to GAO's 2002 study of this market. Small employers buy coverage in this market, and its health shapes what workers pay. For each state and the District of Columbia, GAO counted the carriers licensed to sell small group plans. It named the largest carriers in each state. It also reported each large carrier's share of its state market.

The letter is a data reference rather than a policy argument. Its tables let readers compare how crowded or concentrated each state's market was in 2004. A market ruled by one or two carriers raises different concerns than a crowded field. Lawmakers use such counts when they weigh rules for small business health coverage. The update keeps the 2002 baseline current for that debate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-255r:
The price of auditing internal controls across government is weighed in GAO-06-255R, a letter report dated September 6, 2006. A 2004 law on the Homeland Security Department's finances set this study in motion. Two councils, of finance chiefs and of integrity officials, jointly weighed the costs and gains. Their question: should all big agencies have to win an auditor's opinion on their internal controls? The same law told the Comptroller General to review that study and report to Congress.

GAO briefed committee staff on an early read in December 2005. This letter gives the fuller analysis. It shares GAO's views on whether such opinions should be required. Internal control opinions are standard for big firms under recent corporate law. Extending them across government would cost money and staff time. The gain would be sharper proof that agency books rest on sound systems. The letter helps Congress size that trade before it acts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-355r:
Ranchers graze livestock on some national park land, and the fee rules were fuzzy. A GAO letter, GAO-06-355R of February 9, 2006, follows up on grazing in the National Park Service. Grazing took place on nearly 1.6 million acres at 31 park units. In fiscal year 2004 the units spent at least $410,000 to manage it and took in about $196,000.

GAO found park units did not apply permit guidance in a steady way. Fees, cost recovery, and keeping receipts all varied. The letter urges clearer and stronger guidance on setting fees. It also covers how cost-recovery sums should be reported and kept. Readers see a small fee system with wide gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-365r:
Two Gulf hurricanes left a huge federal response to judge. Statement GAO-06-365R, dated February 1, 2006, gives early GAO views on Hurricanes Katrina and Rita. Comptroller General David M Walker presented the statement. GAO had begun a broad body of work on the storms. It covered federal, state, and local levels.

The statement deals with how well officials prepared. It also covers the response once the storms hit and the start of recovery. GAO calls the findings preliminary, not final. That caution is part of the record's value. Readers get an early, careful account of what GAO saw. Later GAO work would build on these first observations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-455r:
A stealth fighter built for a Soviet threat was gaining new missions. Letter report GAO-06-455R, dated June 20, 2006, reviews the F-22A program. The jet has a stealth, highly mobile airframe and a new engine. It can fly at supersonic speed without afterburners. It was meant to replace the F-15 in air-to-air combat. The Air Force now plans added ground attack and intelligence roles.

Those roles were not part of the first design. Counts and funding have shifted since the program began in 1986. GAO judged the need for a fresh business case before more investment. It also tested legal criteria for a multiyear contract. Readers get the case for pausing to rethink.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-505r:
Mothers who lost sons or daughters in service keep a chartered group. Letter GAO-06-505R, dated March 14, 2006, reviews the audit of American Gold Star Mothers, Incorporated. The audit covers fiscal years 2003 and 2002. The group's purpose is to perpetuate the ideals of Americanism. Those are the ideals for which members' loved ones fought and died, the letter states.

Chartered corporations must file yearly statements and obtain an independent audit. GAO read the statements and the auditor's report. It found no reportable instance of noncompliance. The auditor said the statements were presented fairly. They were kept on a modified cash basis of accounting. Readers get a brief audit result.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-545r:
Undercover teams carried radioactive sources across the border to test the detectors. Letter report GAO-06-545R, dated March 28, 2006, reports that investigation. Congress asked GAO to probe weaknesses in radiation detection gear at U.S. ports of entry. The test focused on portal monitors in place at those ports. It asked whether the monitors would detect radioactive material in vehicles entering the country. GAO also watched how Customs and Border Protection inspectors acted when monitors alarmed.

The title gives the result. Investigators successfully transported the sources across at selected locations. Readers get a rare direct test of border equipment. Earlier GAO work on the northern border is noted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-685r:
Financial reporting by the American Ex-Prisoners of War is checked in GAO letter report GAO-06-685R, dated May 12, 2006. The group serves Americans who were held as prisoners of war and holds a federal charter. Its fiscal year 2003 statements were audited by an independent public accountant, as federal law requires of chartered corporations. GAO's task was to scan the audit for any matters Congress should know about.

GAO reviewed the audit reports covering those statements. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance with the law's financial reporting rules. One detail sets this review apart from its neighbors. The auditor judged the statements fairly presented on a modified cash basis of accounting, not the usual accrual basis. GAO's letter notes the opinion and closes the yearly check.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-725r:
Military training ranges get a progress report in GAO-06-725R, a letter report GAO issued on June 20, 2006. A 2003 defense law told the Secretary of Defense to build a full plan for sustaining training ranges. Urban growth, lawsuits, and other limits had squeezed the land and airspace where troops train. The law listed items the plan and yearly reports had to cover. GAO tracked how the department's reporting had evolved.

GAO found continued improvement in the reporting on sustainable ranges. Still, some required items were missing, such as a full judgment of whether resources meet training needs. The reports also lacked recommendations for legal changes to ease training limits. GAO said more time was needed to put key initiatives fully in place. The letter keeps pressure on a slow reform.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-835r:
Adding nations to visa-free travel is explained in GAO-06-835R, a letter report dated July 28, 2006. The Visa Waiver Program lets citizens of 27 nations visit the United States for tourism or business for 90 days or less without a visa. It speeds travel while aiming to protect national security. In fiscal year 2004, more than 15 million travelers entered under its terms. Allied nations pressed to join the program.

GAO described the process for admitting new countries. The Homeland Security Department was drafting formal procedures to guide admissions. Until they are final, an interim process applies. Under it, the Secretary of Homeland Security, consulting the Secretary of State, may designate a new member country. The letter gives lawmakers a clear map of a sensitive gatekeeping task.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-925r:
Catholic War Veterans of the United States of America has its yearly audit noted in GAO letter GAO-06-925R, dated July 7, 2006. The group's aims take in care for veterans and their widows and orphans, and defense of the Constitution. It holds a federal charter, so its accounts face an outside audit.

GAO read the audit report for fiscal year 2004. The auditors held that the statements were fairly shown under U.S. accounting rules. GAO found no breach that had to be reported. Short as it is, the letter puts that audit outcome on the record for Congress and for the charter file.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1165r:
U.S. presence at world air shows is traced in GAO letter GAO-07-1165R, dated September 21, 2007. Shows in Paris and at Farnborough let firms show craft and win deals worth billions. Federal agencies rent space, show planes, and aid U.S. aerospace firms there. Big U.S. firms are well seen. The place of small and mid-size firms is less clear.

GAO named which agencies took part since 2000, and what aid they gave U.S. firms. It asked what drives small and mid-size firms to go, or stay home. U.S. presence, it found, rests chiefly on agency missions and on what firms can spare.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-215r:
Before awarding a contract, agencies must judge whether a firm is responsible enough to hold it. GAO looked at one screening tool in GAO-07-215R, a letter dated January 12, 2007. Congress worried about fraud by contractors with criminal pasts. GAO asked selected agencies how they make responsibility calls. It asked when they run criminal background checks. It also studied the excluded parties list and fraud case data.

Federal rules neither require nor bar criminal checks for this purpose, GAO found. Officers said they check the excluded parties list for banned firms. They run pre-award surveys on larger contracts. They weigh past performance, skill, finances, and ethics. The letter's enclosure holds data on suspensions and debarments from fiscal years 1996 through 2006. It also reports how many fraud probes involved contractors with prior records. The work ran from June through October 2006.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-235r:
A new Congress was about to take office, and GAO offered it a work list. GAO sent the list in GAO-07-235R, a letter dated November 17, 2006. The letter holds three sets of suggestions for the 110th Congress. The first set names targets for near-term oversight. The second set names programs needing deep reform and rebuilding. The third set covers governance issues for the whole government. An enclosure gives the detail behind each item.

GAO framed the list around its three roles: oversight, insight, and foresight. It drew the items from its body of audit work across agencies. It urged oversight that holds officials to account for results. It also urged hearings that spread good practice between agencies. The goal stated in the letter is a government that works in an economical and ethical way. The suggestions were offered for planning the new Congress's agenda.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-295r: Indian trust funds have drawn qualified audit opinions every year since 1996. GAO reported on the cleanup backlog in GAO-07-295R, dated January 19, 2007. A 1994 law recognized federal duties toward American Indians. It created a trustee office inside the Interior Department. That office prepares the trust funds' financial statements. Congress asked GAO to check two things. It wanted the status of audit fixes from fiscal years 1996 through 2005. It also wanted a judgment on follow-up controls. The letter sends Congress the slides from GAO's October 5, 2006 briefing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-325r: The Gold Star Wives of America holds a federal charter, so GAO reviews its outside audits. GAO-07-325R, a letter dated January 26, 2007, covers audits for fiscal years 2006 and 2005. In both years, the auditor held that the group's statements were presented fairly under U.S. accounting rules. GAO found no breaches worth reporting in the reports it reviewed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-475r:
Colonial history is the cause of the National Society, Daughters of the American Colonists, and GAO-07-475R, a GAO letter of March 9, 2007, reviews its audit. The society studies, publishes, and marks the history and deeds of American colonists. It is a federally chartered corporation. Under 36 U.S.C. 10101 it must file yearly statements of assets, debts, income, and costs, and it must obtain an outside audit.

The letter covers the fiscal years ended December 31, 2005 and 2004. GAO read the audit report and the statements behind it and ran checks on the figures. It did not audit the society or render its own opinion. The review found no reportable noncompliance with the law. The auditor's opinion said the statements were fairly presented under standard accounting rules. The letter is brief, as are all in this charter series.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-485r:
Billions for outbreak readiness need proof of progress, and GAO-07-485R, dated March 23, 2007, traces how that proof gets measured. From 2002 to 2006, Congress gave about $6.1 billion to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for preparedness. The money flows each year to 62 recipients, all 50 states plus 4 large cities among them. Two programs share the work, one at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and one for hospitals.

GAO followed how the scoring systems for both programs changed over time. It asked how the agencies use the scores to judge gains. Early measures counted plans and gear more than real skill. Katrina's weak response and flu fears sharpened the debate. The letter shows a slow shift toward tests that show what states can actually do, not just what they own.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-665r:
The American stage has a chartered academy, and GAO-07-665R, issued April 5, 2007, reviews its audit. The American National Theatre and Academy presents plays. It works to grow interest in drama, back the best new productions, and build the craft of theatre. It holds a federal charter, so it must present yearly financial statements in set detail and obtain an audit by an outside public accountant.

The letter covers the fiscal years ended June 30, 2004 and 2003. GAO read the audit reports and the statements behind them. It ran checks on the figures but did not perform an audit or render its own opinion. No instance of noncompliance worth reporting came to light. The auditors' opinions said the statements were fairly presented under U.S. accounting standards. GAO returned the reports, closing the yearly check for this charter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-675r:
Military freight learns from a failed pilot in GAO-07-675R, a GAO letter report of May 8, 2007. The Defense Department ships freight from over 600 sites to thousands of points in the continental United States. The bill runs about $900 million a year. In 2001 it tested a third-party logistics firm at sites in the Southeast. The Defense Logistics Agency stayed with the pilot; the services quit it, unhappy with the work.

The lessons fed a bigger build, the Defense Transportation Coordination Initiative. A contract sought in June 2006 would hand freight to one logistics partner. By the end of 2009, 67 sites join; almost 200 more may follow. Freight at those sites runs about $250 million a year. The department projects savings of about $60 million in the third year, before management costs. GAO found the lessons well used and urged the department to spread what it learns next.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1025r:
Health screening of troops after deployment is examined in GAO report GAO-08-1025R, issued September 4, 2008. The post-deployment health reassessment screens servicemembers 90 to 180 days after they return from combat tours. It aims to catch health problems, including mental health problems, that surface late. The Defense Department set the screening rules in March 2005.

Army research had shown that more troops report mental health concerns months after return than right away. GAO checked how the services track completion of the screening. It found that oversight of completion rates is limited. That gap leaves the department unsure that all returning troops get screened and referred for care when needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1055r:
A mandated review of air cargo screening exemptions is transmitted in GAO report GAO-08-1055R (August 15, 2008). A 2007 law told the Comptroller General to assess how the Secretary of Homeland Security handles these exemptions. The law in question allows some cargo to skip standard screening. GAO judged the method used to keep, change, or drop each exemption.

GAO shared a restricted version of its briefing with the named committees in July 2008. This public version removes all material the security agency classed as sensitive. GAO made no recommendations for Congress or the agency. The report preserves the briefing that met the law's deadline.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1075r:
Laws guarding private computer systems in vital sectors are cataloged in GAO letter GAO-08-1075R, dated September 16, 2008. Federal policy names 18 sectors as critical infrastructure. They span banking, energy, health care, and telecom networks, among others. Most of this infrastructure is owned by private firms. All of it leans heavily on computer systems and data.

Congress asked GAO to map the rules that guard those systems. For each sector, GAO lists the federal laws, regulations, and binding standards that apply. It also names how each rule is enforced. The letter gives lawmakers a single map of a scattered legal field.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-155r:
Follow-up answers on care for deployed civilians form GAO report GAO-08-155R, dated October 16, 2007. GAO had testified on September 18, 2007, before a House armed services subcommittee. The topic was benefits and medical care for federal civilian and contract staff sent to Iraq and Afghanistan. Members filed further questions for the record.

The report answers two of them. One asks what rules Congress has set for tracking the health of deployed troops and civilians. The other asks what work GAO has done on the topic. The answers give lawmakers a compact brief on a niche but vital duty of care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-295r:
Repayment of court awards by agencies is tracked in GAO letter GAO-08-295R, dated February 26, 2008. A central Judgment Fund, set up in 1956, pays court judgments against federal agencies at once. Two laws then make agencies pay the fund back. A 2002 act covers discrimination and whistleblower cases. A 1978 act covers contract disputes. The payback rule aims to make agencies answer for their own wrongs.

The 2002 act told GAO to study payments and repayments under both laws. This letter reports the status of those reimbursements. It shows how fully agencies have settled their debts to the fund. The record feeds Congress's watch on agency accountability.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-365r:
International pledges to rebuild Iraq are tallied in GAO correspondence GAO-08-365R, dated December 18, 2007. Members of a House appropriations subcommittee had asked for updated figures after an October 30, 2007 hearing on U.S. efforts in Iraq. The letter breaks pledges down by donor country, loans, and grants.

Donors had pledged about $16.4 billion for Iraq reconstruction, with about $13.6 billion of it offered at the October 2003 donor conference in Madrid. Most nations pledged grants, but most of the money came as loans. The largest loan pledges came from Japan, at $3.4 billion, the World Bank, at $3 billion, and the International Monetary Fund, at up to $2.55 billion. The tables give each donor's pledge and what had been provided as of October 2007.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-495r:
Joint health care work by two departments is tracked in GAO letter GAO-08-495R, dated April 30, 2008. A President's task force set up on May 28, 2001 gave 20 recommendations on how the Departments of Veterans Affairs and Defense should share care and resources. GAO graded how far each one has come.

Seven recommendations are fully in place and 11 are partly done. One could not be graded for lack of information, and one needs no department action. Full wins include a joint council that reports each year and joint health outcome metrics. Partial steps cover shared electronic medical records, a single separation physical, and pharmacy teamwork. The letter builds on barriers GAO has long noted, such as clashing computer systems and uneven payment rules between the two systems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-565r:
Condom label review is the topic of GAO letter GAO-08-565R, dated April 25, 2008. Sexually transmitted diseases bring an estimated 19 million new infections a year in the United States. A provision in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2001 ordered the health department to recheck condom labels for medical accuracy.

The Food and Drug Administration did the review. It found that current labels lack full information on how well condoms block certain diseases. Condoms guard less well against human papillomavirus, which spreads by more routes, than against some other infections. Used right and every time, they still cut transmission risk. The law required only the recheck, so the agency complied. It has since started rule changes to improve the labels.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-595r:
Wastewater treatment at the Mexican border is covered in GAO letter GAO-08-595R, dated April 24, 2008. Untreated sewage from Tijuana flows into the United States through the Tijuana River and out to the Pacific, closing southern California beaches. The South Bay plant in San Ysidro has given 25 million gallons a day only primary treatment since 1997.

The plant's secondary treatment stage was never built, so its discharge has never met Clean Water Act rules. A court order demands compliance by September 30, 2008. Two paths remain: upgrade the San Ysidro plant to secondary treatment on site, or build a new plant in Mexico, as Bajagua, LLC proposes, to treat the partly cleaned flow. The letter compares the two for the boundary commission.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-625r:
The Bureau of the Public Debt keeps the books on what the United States owes. Safe computers matter, since its systems handle the federal debt schedules. GAO-08-625R, a letter dated May 27, 2008, reports flaws found in the bureau's computer security controls during the yearly debt audit.

Auditors still found the bureau's core controls sound overall for the debt schedules as of September 30, 2007. The flaws they did find were not classed as major gaps. Guards, watch tools, and cross-checks by hand cut the risk. Even so, GAO listed fixes the bureau should make and checked on fixes promised in past audits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-735r:
U.S. funds repay Pakistan for army operations against terrorists along the Afghan border. GAO-08-735R, a letter dated May 6, 2008, gives early notes on those Coalition Support Funds and the checks on them. Final findings were due in summer 2008.

From October 2001 through June 2007, repayments came to about $5.56 billion. The cash goes straight into Pakistan's treasury and becomes its own funds, beyond U.S. watch. Before payment, U.S. staff in Pakistan review claims, and commanders confirm the operations aided U.S. missions. Cost checks compare claims with like U.S. costs. The letter maps that chain and its limits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-85r:
First-class and business-class flights by farm agency staff drew charges of abuse. GAO-08-85R, a management letter dated November 19, 2007, gives six fix proposals. It grows out of a September 2007 report on premium travel at the Agriculture Department.

The department spent over $110 million on air travel in the span checked, with about $3.9 million touching a premium seat. One arm, the Foreign Agricultural Service, flew premium nearly 30 percent of the time and took $2.0 million of that spend. Of 145 premium trips checked, 140 lacked papers to justify the upgrade. Some were approved by staff below the traveler.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-965r:
Security clearance reform is the subject of GAO-08-965R, a July 2008 letter answering three questions for the record after May 2008 testimony. Lawmakers asked about quality in the clearance process, how the defense clearance agency forecasts its workload, and related reform steps. The letter answers from GAO's clearance work dating back years.

On quality, GAO repeats its call for quality checks across all six phases of the process, from setting requirements to updating clearances. Weak quality is why agencies often refuse to honor each other's clearances. On forecasting, the Defense Security Service's yearly contractor survey is improving but still evolving. GAO also notes two new reviews: one of the joint reform team's plan, and one of defense clearance quality and timeliness.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-985r:
Debris still left from Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans is the focus of GAO-08-985R, dated August 25, 2008. The 2005 storm killed more than 1,600 people and drove over a million from their homes. By July 2008 the Federal Emergency Management Agency had funded about 16,900 home tear-downs. State officials said about 6,100 homes still waited.

The report lays out how federal and state agencies oversee the cleanup, what fines and orders they have used, and how they dealt with health fears at the Gentilly Landfill. It also covers the Chef Menteur Landfill and a pilot project that cut debris in St. Bernard Parish. Readers get a clear view of a cleanup still far from done, three years on.
